title: Datadog API: Keys, Endpoints, and Getting Started
summary: Datadog API is an HTTP/JSON interface from regional domains callable via scripts and workflows. You'll understand authentication setup and rate limits.
body_markdown:
## Call the same Datadog endpoints with Activepieces


Activepieces can call the same Datadog endpoints for low-volume jobs like creating an event, muting a monitor or sending an incident to chat.


It takes the same scoped keys and obeys the same limits you already read about, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, against 1,000 credits a month on the free plan.


### When a no-code workflow is enough


Batching cuts the calls that cause 429s, but some calls are better not written as code at all.


When an incident opens, a workflow can post a summary to a chat channel and mute a noisy monitor, which is a handful of requests per trigger.


That's a good fit for Activepieces, since you can generate a integration for the endpoint with AI and add it privately to your own instance, and flows are unlimited on every plan, including free.


The screenshot below shows the shape of such a flow in a different app. It has a trigger, then one HTTP request step that POSTs to a revoke endpoint with an Authorization header.


The run details panel on the left holds the JSON in and out of each step.


When a run fails, read that panel first, because it shows the status and body the API actually returned. A Datadog flow looks the same, with a Datadog URL and Datadog's key headers.


### What a workflow doesn't replace


High-volume intake is what it doesn't replace. Streaming logs, metrics or traces through a workflow engine means one execution per event, and you'll hit rate limits you can't tune from inside a flow.


That traffic belongs in the Datadog Agent or in code that batches and backs off.


Rate limits still apply to a flow. A 429 inside a step is a failed step, so decide what the flow should do about it: add a retry on the step, or let the run fail visibly so someone checks it.


Silent loops are the worse outcome.


### Use the scoped key in the connection


Build the connection with an application key scoped to what the flow does, not the over-powered key you use elsewhere. A flow that only creates events needs permission to create events. A flow that mutes monitors needs monitor write access and nothing broader.


If the flow's credentials leak through a shared workspace or a copied template, the damage stops at that scope.


In the HTTP step, set the API key and application key as headers, using the connection's stored values rather than pasting them into the step. Keep one connection per flow purpose so you can revoke one without breaking the rest.


Then read the response headers in the run details. They show your remaining budget for that endpoint, which is the number to check before you add a second trigger to the same flow.
